subtype: Approach: allowing feelings and staying with family [Thinking]
passage:
Monday. The call came during maths. Thatha had collapsed in the garden and was gone before the ambulance arrived. At home, Lakshmi's cousin Arohi was already crying on the stairs. Lakshmi's first thought was: don't cry in front of everyone, be useful. She held it in for an hour, then broke down in the bathroom, sobbing into a towel.
Wednesday. During the rituals Lakshmi sat on the floor with Paati and the aunts, not doing much, just there. When the priest said Thatha's name, the tears came again. Hiding it doesn't make it smaller, she thought. Everyone here is sad. I'm allowed to be too. This time she let them fall in front of everyone, and Paati squeezed her hand.
Two Sundays later. Arohi asked, "Are you over it yet?" Lakshmi shook her head. "I don't think it works like that. I think I just keep sitting with it."

qa.a: Thatha collapsed in the garden.

qa.q: Why did Lakshmi hold back tears on Monday?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt she had to be strong and useful and was afraid of crying in front of everyone, so the grief burst out alone in the bathroom.

qa.q: What else could help Lakshmi in the weeks ahead?
qa.a: Lakshmi could keep spending time with Paati sharing memories of Thatha, and talk to a trusted adult if the sadness ever feels too heavy to carry.

qa.q: How might Paati experience Lakshmi crying beside her?
qa.a: Paati may feel less alone in her own grief, and the hand squeeze suggests she is comforted that Lakshmi isn't hiding it.

grounding: Shows a teen letting herself cry and sitting with the family through the rituals after her grandfather's sudden death, seeing that grief cannot be rushed or hidden.

subtype: Approach: allowing feelings and staying with family [Thinking]
passage: Sit, Jyoti. You asked why I light a lamp for my own thatha every Deepavali. I was fifteen when he died, just like that, at his shop counter in Salem. That evening everyone told me, "Rukmini, don't cry, your amma needs you strong." So I didn't. I made coffee, I swept, I kept my face like stone. On the third day my Periamma found me behind the well, shaking. She didn't scold. She sat down in the dirt beside me and said, "Cry, kanna. He was your thatha too." And I cried until my throat hurt. After that I sat with the family through every ritual, and I cried whenever it came. Grief is not a guest you can hurry out of the house, Jyoti. I learned that behind a well, and it has stayed with me all these years.

qa.q: Where did Rukmini's thatha die?
qa.a: He died at his shop counter in Salem.

qa.q: What was Rukmini feeling while keeping a face like stone?
qa.a: Rukmini was grieving but felt pressured to be strong, holding the sadness in until it came out as shaking behind the well.

qa.q: What turning point changed how Rukmini grieved?

subtype: Approach: taking on practical tasks for the family [Action]
passage: When Chachu died on the highway, our house in Lucknow filled up in a single afternoon. I'm Irfan. I didn't know what to do with my hands, so I found jobs. I answered the landline and wrote every caller's name in a notebook for Dadi. I carried water jugs from the tanker to the kitchen, three at a time. When the little cousins started running between the adults' legs, I took them up to the terrace with a ball. My cousin Indu came up with tea at sunset and asked if I was okay. I said, "I'm fine, I'm busy." Then the ball rolled against Chachu's old bicycle, and I sat down on the steps and cried. Indu sat beside me. Looking back, the jobs gave me something to hold, but they didn't stop me missing him. They weren't supposed to.

qa.q: What did Irfan write in the notebook for Dadi?
qa.a: Irfan wrote every caller's name.

qa.q: What was Irfan feeling when the ball hit Chachu's bicycle?
qa.a: Irfan's grief broke through; the busy, fine feeling gave way to missing Chachu, and the tears came.

qa.a: Irfan could take short breaks to sit with family or talk with Indu about Chachu, so the tasks shape the day without replacing time to be sad.

Saturday. Written by Francis's godparent, for the family's memory book.
Since Friday morning, when Mary Ammachi died so suddenly in her sleep, Francis has barely sat down. He took over the gate, greeting people from the parish and showing them where to leave their chappals. He answered the phone, which rang every ten minutes, and kept a list of who would bring food on which day. When his little cousin Uday started crying because nobody would tell him where Ammachi had gone, Francis took him onto his lap and told him simply that she had died and wasn't coming back, and that it was okay to be sad.
Late at night I found Francis in the kitchen, holding Ammachi's steel tumbler, eyes wet. I didn't say anything. I just sat with him. Tomorrow, after the funeral mass, I'll make sure he gets a proper rest.

For a week I told no one at school. I just sat in class like a stone. Then my friend Shobha asked why I'd stopped eating lunch, and something cracked. I told her everything, right there under the neem tree. The same day, she walked me to Rizvi Sir, our maths teacher. He closed the staffroom door and said, "Seema, take your time." I told them both how Abbu hummed old songs while ironing, how he saved the newspaper crossword for me. Talking didn't bring him back, beta. But from that day I wasn't carrying him alone any more.

passage: Hafsa's father died on the night the first heavy snow fell on Srinagar. For two days the roads were shut, the mobile network kept dropping, and school stayed closed. Hafsa sat by the kangri with her mother and aunts, hearing the same condolences, saying nothing of her own. On the third morning school reopened. At the gate, Irfan asked why she hadn't answered any messages. She opened her mouth to say "network" and instead said, "Papa died." Irfan didn't rush to fill the silence. He walked with her to the staffroom, where Ms. Wani, their class teacher, made space on a bench. Hafsa found herself telling them about Papa: how he fixed every radio in the mohalla, how he pretended to lose at carrom. By the end, her shoulders had come down.

subtype: Approach: adjusting study and exam plans with school support [Action]
passage: Two weeks after his Amma's sudden death, Jagdish still couldn't finish a single page of homework. The fields needed him before school, his little sister needed him after, and at night the house was too quiet to think. On Monday he waited behind after class at the government high school in Hosakote. "Sangeeta Madam, I can't keep up right now." She put down her chalk and listened. Together they looked at what was due: a science project, two maths worksheets, the Kannada essay. "The essay can wait three weeks," she said. "Do one maths sheet this week, not two. I'll speak to the science teacher." Jagdish wrote a new plan in his notebook: one subject a night, forty minutes, then sleep. The first week, he finished everything on it. It wasn't much, but it was done.

subtype: Approach: adjusting study and exam plans with school support [Action]
passage: Bao's grandmother died of a stroke on a Thursday, three weeks before the mid-year exams. She had lived with them in the flat above the bakery in Footscray and walked Bao to school for nine years. By the next Tuesday, Bao had read the same history chapter five times without remembering a line. At lunch, Priscila watched Bao stare at an untouched sandwich. "You should tell Mr. Hale." "Everyone's got exams." "Everyone's grandmother didn't just die." That afternoon Bao went to the homeroom teacher's desk. Mr. Hale listened, then pulled up the calendar. They moved the history essay and the science report back three weeks. Bao crossed out the old study timetable and made a smaller one: an hour a day, one subject, Sundays off. It felt like cheating at first. By Friday, it felt like breathing.

subtype: Approach: suppressing emotion to seem strong [Pitfall]
passage: I live across the corridor from Nilesh's family, so I saw more than I was meant to. At his father's funeral, an uncle gripped Nilesh's shoulder and said, "You're the man of this house now. No crying." Nilesh nodded. He didn't cry once that I saw. For weeks after, he was everywhere: fixing the leaking tap, fetching gas cylinders, carrying his sister Charu's school bag, studying at the window till one in the morning. People in the building said, "So strong, that boy." Then, a month later, I heard shouting through the wall. Nilesh had thrown his geometry box at the door because Charu used his ruler. Charu was crying. After that his light stayed on all night, most nights. I don't know what was going on inside him. But he didn't look strong. He looked like someone holding his breath.

Day of the funeral. Dadaji put a heavy hand on Hemant's back. "You're the man of this family now. Men don't cry in front of others." Hemant swallowed hard and went to arrange the chairs. That night he ironed his school uniform and did two chapters of physics.
Three weeks later. Hemant had not missed a single homework, but in class he snapped at Rahul for borrowing his eraser, then stared at the desk, shocked at himself. Sabina Ma'am noticed the dark circles.
Five weeks later. He had barely slept all week. At home he shouted at his little brother over the TV remote and slammed the door so hard a photo frame fell. Papa's photo. He picked it up and couldn't let go. Next morning Sabina Ma'am asked him to stay after class. "I'm fine, Ma'am," he said. "I have to be." She didn't let it go, and that afternoon she called his mother.

Housemaster's note, Sunday.
Tenzin's mother and uncle visited today, three weeks after his Mola's death. They brought a small album and a khata she had kept. The moment his mother opened the album in the visitors' room, Tenzin stood up, said he had football, and left. His mother sat holding the book, looking hurt.
This fits what I've seen. He took Mola's framed photo off his locker the day after the news. When boys in his dorm mention her, he walks out. He sleeps badly and snaps at small things. Avoiding every reminder isn't dulling the pain; it seems to keep it raw, and keeps his family outside it.
Next steps: I spoke with his mother before she left. I'll ask the school counsellor to see him this week, and she'll phone him on Wednesday, just to talk, no album.
Kishore Sir

Thursday night
Vidya put Appa's photo back on the shelf again today. I had moved it into the cupboard on Monday, with his watch and the old cricket cap. I can't walk past his face every time I get water.
At dinner Amma said, "Appa would have liked this rasam," and I got up and went to my room. Vidya followed and stood in the doorway. "You always leave. We want to talk about him. You act like he never existed." I told her to get out.
It's been two months. I thought if I didn't look or listen, it would fade. It doesn't. Tonight I heard Amma and Vidya laughing in the kitchen about his terrible jokes, and it hurt worse than anything, because I wasn't in there with them.
Shankar

14 January
Biji would have been seventy-eight today.
This morning I wrote her a letter. I told her about my science marks, the new calf at Mamaji's farm, how Mummy still hums her songs while cooking. I folded it into her old prayer book.
In the evening we lit a diya by her photo, Mummy, Papa, Veer and me. Nobody said much, but nobody left either.
Then we made her kadhi. Mummy read out Biji's handwritten recipe and I stirred, and it split because I stopped stirring, just like Biji always warned. We all laughed. My friend Kishore came by with his mother, and we fed them too.
I think we'll do this every year. The letter, the diya, the kadhi. It feels like she's still in the kitchen with us, a little.
Amandeep

qa.a: Amandeep folded it into Biji's old prayer book.

qa.q: How did Amandeep feel when the kadhi split?
qa.a: Amandeep felt a warm, bittersweet closeness, laughing with the family because Biji had always warned about exactly that.

qa.q: What else could keep this tradition meaningful as the years pass?
qa.a: The family could let each person add something, like a memory read aloud, so the ritual grows with them.

qa.q: How might Mummy experience the day?
qa.a: Mummy, who still hums Biji's songs, gets to remember her mother openly with the family, reading the recipe and laughing together.

grounding: Shows a teen writing a letter to a dead grandmother, lighting a lamp on her birthday and cooking her dish with the family as a lasting remembrance.

subtype: Approach: noticing when grief becomes overwhelming and seeking support [Revision]
passage:
Tuesday, 11 pm
Five months since Appachan died, and I still read the same page of chemistry four times. I lie awake till two, then sleep through the alarm. Ujjwal asked today why I don't come for football any more. I said I'm tired. That's true, but it's not the whole thing.
I kept thinking it would pass. Everyone said the first months are hard. But it isn't getting lighter. It's getting heavier.
So tonight, when Amma was sitting with her tea, I told her. Not everything, but enough: the not sleeping, the chemistry, how I feel like I'm underwater. She put her cup down and held my hand. She said it isn't weakness, it's a lot of grief, and that tomorrow she'll call Mrs. Thomas, the school counsellor, to set up a talk. Then she stayed up with me till I felt sleepy.
Jomon

qa.a: Amma sees it as a lot of grief rather than weakness, and responds that night by holding Jomon's hand and planning to call the counsellor.

passage:
First evening after the thirteenth-day ceremony. The relatives had gone. Sameer found his mother, Tanuja, sitting on the balcony in the dark. He wanted to say something wise. Everything he thought of, "He's in a better place," "Be strong, Mummy," sounded hollow. So he made two cups of tea and sat beside her. They didn't talk.
A week later. Same balcony. This time she spoke first, about how Papa used to burn the toast every Sunday. Sameer just listened, and laughed when she laughed. When she cried, he didn't try to stop it. He passed her the dupatta she'd dropped.
A month later. His aunt Mahima phoned, asking if Tanuja was "over the worst." Sameer glanced at the balcony, where two cups already waited. "She's still sad," he said. "We sit together in the evenings. That helps."

qa.a: Papa used to burn the toast every Sunday.

qa.q: Why did Sameer stay silent on the first evening?

qa.a: Sameer could gently ask whether she wants to talk or just sit, and let Mahima or another adult share some evenings, so he isn't carrying it alone.

qa.q: How does Tanuja experience the evenings on the balcony?

subtype: Approach: supporting a grieving family member [Action]
passage: Swati beti, you asked how to help your aunt now that her husband has gone. Let me tell you about my Faisal. When his abba died, Faisal was fourteen. The whole mohalla came with advice: "Be patient, Rehana," "Keep yourself busy," "Time heals." Everyone talked. Faisal didn't. Every evening after namaz he came to my room with two cups of chai and sat on the floor by my feet. Some nights I talked about his abba's silly rhymes. Some nights I only cried. He never said, "Don't cry, Ammi." Once I asked him, "Why don't you say anything?" He said, "I don't know what to say, so I'm just staying." That staying, beti, did more for me than all the advice in the mohalla put together.

qa.a: Choosing to sit with his mother every evening with chai, without advice or telling her not to cry, because it let her talk or weep as she needed.

qa.a: The advice felt like a lot of talk, while Faisal's quiet staying comforted her far more than all of it together.

subtype: Approach: adapting routines to a changed household [Revision]
passage: When Abbu died last March, the tailoring shop closed for a month and everything at home shifted. I'm Nazia. At first I decided, alone, that I'd drop tuition and stay home to help Ammi. I didn't ask anyone. Two weeks later Ammi found out and was upset. So one Sunday we sat down properly: Ammi, Khala, Nani and Pranav bhaiya, who had worked in Abbu's shop for six years. Pranav bhaiya said he could keep the shop open in the mornings if Ammi handled the orders. Khala offered to take my little brother to school. My part became evening cooking and helping with the order book, not quitting tuition. In June, when orders dropped in the rains, we met again and moved tuition to weekends for two months. Looking back, the plan kept changing, and that was fine, because we changed it together.

qa.q: How long had Pranav bhaiya worked in Abbu's shop?
qa.a: He had worked there for six years.

qa.q: Why do you think Nazia first decided alone to drop tuition?
qa.a: Nazia likely felt anxious and responsible for helping Ammi after Abbu's death, and rushed into a big decision without asking anyone.

qa.q: What else could keep the plan working as things change?
qa.a: The family could set a regular time to review chores and schooling together, so problems are caught before anyone quietly gives something up.

qa.q: How did Ammi see Nazia's plan to drop tuition?
qa.a: Ammi was upset, since she didn't want Nazia giving up studies alone, and this led the family to decide things together.

grounding: Shows a teen, after a parent's death changes income and duties, working out chores and schooling with relatives and revising the plan as things change.

subtype: Approach: adapting routines to a changed household [Revision]
passage:
Class teacher's note, Lavanya (Class 10), 3 August.
Since her mother's death in May, Lavanya's father has taken night shifts at the mill and her grandmother has moved in. Lavanya came to me last week, worried she would have to leave school to look after her brother Saurabh, who is in Class 2.
Today her father and grandmother came in with her, and we talked it through together. Paati will manage the mornings and get Saurabh to school; Lavanya will pick him up and help with his homework; her father will cook on his days off. Lavanya asked if her tuition could move to Saturdays, and we agreed.
Update, 1 September: Paati's knees make the morning walk hard. The family met again and changed the plan: a neighbour now walks Saurabh to school with her own children. Lavanya has not missed a class.

qa.q: Who will pick Saurabh up from school?
qa.a: Lavanya will pick him up.

qa.q: What was Lavanya worried about when she first came to the teacher?
qa.a: Lavanya was worried about having to leave school to look after Saurabh.

qa.q: What else could help keep the family's plan workable?
qa.a: They could keep meeting whenever something changes and tell the teacher, so Lavanya's schooling is protected each time.

qa.q: How might Paati see the change on 1 September?
qa.a: Paati may feel relieved that her painful knees are taken into account, while still being part of caring for the children.

grounding: Illustrates a teen and her family meeting with the teacher to rearrange chores and schooling after her mother's death, then revising the plan a month later.
